identity.name: MOSAIC
identity.tagline: Partnerships work when trust moves at the speed of business.
identity.description: A 25-item assessment that measures a leader's effectiveness in cross-border institutional partnerships across four dimensions: institutional trust, relationship velocity, normative flexibility, and conflict resolution. The assessment focuses on partnership capability in contexts where institutional frameworks differ, AI adoption rates are asymmetric, and relationship quality determines commercial outcomes.
identity.ideal_use_case: Leaders managing bilateral cross-border partnerships; joint venture and alliance managers; business development leaders in APAC markets; partnership health assessments before strategic alignment.

instrument_spec.delivery_format: Online self-assessment with instant HTML report
instrument_spec.scoring_method: Dimension-level normalised scores (0–20 each) + composite percentile (0–100)

dimensions.name: Institutional Trust
dimensions.description: Measures the leader's ability to build and maintain trust in partnerships where institutional frameworks (legal, regulatory, governance) differ or are less reliable — including awareness of how AI capability asymmetry creates governance risk.
dimensions.what_high_means: The leader understands institutional trust dynamics, builds alternative trust mechanisms when formal frameworks are unreliable, and treats capability asymmetry as a governance risk rather than just an operational difference.
dimensions.what_low_means: The leader relies primarily on contractual frameworks for trust, has not assessed institutional trust degradation, and may not see AI capability asymmetry as a governance concern.

dimensions.name: Relationship Velocity
dimensions.description: Measures the speed and quality with which a leader can build working trust in cross-border relationships — including maintaining relationship quality during disruptions, adapting to AI-driven organisational change, and accelerating relationship rebuilding after setbacks.
dimensions.what_high_means: The leader can establish working trust rapidly, maintains active cross-border networks, adapts relationships when AI changes counterpart organisations, and has clear methods for relationship rebuilding.
dimensions.what_low_means: The leader needs extended time to establish trust, maintains fewer active cross-border relationships, struggles when AI changes counterpart capabilities, and lacks clear rebuilding methods.

dimensions.name: Normative Flexibility
dimensions.description: Measures the leader's ability to identify, adapt to, and operate within unstated normative expectations across different cultural and institutional environments — including how AI capability shifts change what is considered standard professional practice.
dimensions.what_high_means: The leader identifies unstated normative expectations without prompting, adapts their self-presentation as AI changes expectations, and is comfortable making decisions that meet normative expectations in one context but might be interpreted differently in another.
dimensions.what_low_means: The leader struggles with normative uncertainty, has not adapted self-presentation to AI-driven expectation shifts, and finds it difficult to operate when normative expectations are unclear.

dimensions.name: Conflict Resolution
dimensions.description: Measures the leader's ability to diagnose and resolve partnership conflict by distinguishing between interpersonal friction, governance misalignment, and capability asymmetry — including AI-driven capability differences that may appear as cultural or communication issues.
dimensions.what_high_means: The leader distinguishes different types of conflict accurately, has resolved conflicts by addressing underlying capability asymmetry that others missed, and modifies their approach to account for AI-driven friction.
dimensions.what_low_means: The leader tends to escalate conflict rather than resolve it personally, may misattribute capability asymmetry problems to cultural or personal causes, and has not adapted conflict resolution for AI-driven friction.

archetype_framework.logic: Archetypes are defined by which dimensions score in the 'Strong' range (16+/20). High scores in two adjacent dimensions define a primary archetype. Single-dimension high scorers have specialist archetypes.

archetypes.name: The Institutional Strategist
archetypes.core_pattern: Reads institutional environments deeply while building relationships at speed. Most effective cross-border partner type.
strengths: Understands institutional trust dynamics in depth
Builds working trust rapidly in new contexts
Activates partnerships quickly in new markets
growth_areas: May underinvest in normative flexibility — reading unstated expectations
Conflict resolution may rely more on relationship capital than structural diagnosis
Risk of overconfidence in familiar institutional contexts
archetypes.development_focus: Deepen normative flexibility for contexts with different unstated rules; build diagnostic conflict resolution capability beyond relationship-based resolution.
archetypes.organisational_impact: Reduces time-to-value in new market entries and new partnership formations.

archetypes.name: The Deep Connector
archetypes.core_pattern: Builds trust quickly and adapts seamlessly to different normative environments. Strong at maintaining partnership quality across disruptions.
strengths: Reads and adapts to unstated normative expectations
Maintains relationship quality during institutional disruptions
growth_areas: May underestimate institutional trust and governance complexity
Conflict resolution may prioritise harmony over structural resolution
Risk of relationship depth without institutional rigour
archetypes.development_focus: Build institutional trust analysis capability; develop structural conflict diagnosis alongside relational resolution.
archetypes.organisational_impact: Maintains partnership continuity during disruptions. Critical for relationship-dependent revenue streams.

archetypes.name: The Normative Bridge
archetypes.core_pattern: Reads unstated expectations across cultures and resolves conflicts arising from normative misalignment. Critical in APAC partnership contexts.
strengths: Resolves conflicts by addressing normative misalignment root causes
Prevents friction from escalating into structural conflict
growth_areas: May lack deep institutional trust analysis
Relationship velocity may be slower — prioritises quality over speed
archetypes.development_focus: Build institutional trust and governance analysis capability; develop faster relationship establishment methods without sacrificing depth.
archetypes.organisational_impact: Prevents partnership friction from escalating into costly structural conflicts.

archetypes.name: The Capability Broker
archetypes.core_pattern: Understands institutional dynamics deeply and resolves capability asymmetry conflicts effectively. Operates at the governance level of partnerships.
strengths: Deep institutional trust and governance analysis
Addresses root causes of partnership friction rather than symptoms
growth_areas: Relationship velocity may be slower — analytical rather than relational
Normative flexibility may be underdeveloped — relies on structural analysis
Risk of analysing more than connecting
archetypes.development_focus: Build relationship velocity and active network maintenance; develop normative flexibility alongside structural analysis.
archetypes.organisational_impact: Addresses root causes of partnership friction; builds sustainable bilateral governance structures.

archetypes.name: The Relationship Specialist
archetypes.core_pattern: Builds trust quickly but may lack the institutional or normative depth for complex environments. Strong in stable contexts, vulnerable in volatile ones.
growth_areas: Normative flexibility may be shallow — adapts style but not understanding
Conflict resolution relies on relationship capital rather than diagnosis
archetypes.development_focus: Build institutional trust and governance understanding; develop diagnostic conflict resolution capability; deepen normative flexibility.
archetypes.organisational_impact: Effective in familiar partnership contexts. Needs institutional support when operating in novel or rapidly changing environments.

archetypes.name: The Institutional Analyst
archetypes.core_pattern: Deep understanding of institutional dynamics but slower to build relationships or adapt normatively. More analyst than operator.
strengths: Deep institutional trust and governance analysis
Strong risk assessment of institutional trust degradation
Valuable for partnership design and structure
growth_areas: Relationship velocity is slower — needs more time to establish trust
Normative flexibility may be underdeveloped — relies on structural understanding
Conflict resolution may be analytical rather than relational
archetypes.development_focus: Build relationship velocity and active trust-building capability; develop normative flexibility for contexts where rules are unstated.
archetypes.organisational_impact: Valuable for partnership design and governance architecture. Needs relationship-capable partners to execute.

composite_scoring.method: Weighted average of four dimensions, converted to 0–100 composite

bands.interpretation: Mature cross-border partnership capability. Can build institutional trust, develop relationships at speed, and resolve conflicts arising from capability asymmetry.
Moderate cross-border capability with specific dimensions requiring investment. Functional in familiar contexts but may struggle with novel institutional environments.
Foundational cross-border capability is developing but not yet reliable. Significant risk in high-stakes bilateral partnerships.
Significant gaps across all cross-border dimensions. Bilateral partnership effectiveness is at serious risk.

dimension_verdicts.meaning: Emerging cross-border capability with targeted development needs

sections: Primary archetype with organisational impact narrative
report_output.report_format: Interactive HTML report with visual dimension profile
